A Practical 3DGS-to-Vectorworks Workflow

This is Kou Nakamura from Locahun 3D. I first compared 3DGS, a coloured point cloud and a textured mesh from a city-block scan. I then rebuilt a separate hall against its 3DGS and captured images, and imported that editable model into Vectorworks Spotlight 2026. The test separates appearance, measurement, editing and drafting instead of forcing one dataset to do every job.

The conclusion, up frontUse 3DGS for site review, point clouds for measurement and Vectorworks for drafting. The hall OBJ imported successfully, but 1,051 Blender meshes arrived as only four meshes in Vectorworks. It works as shape reference; it does not preserve component-level editability without a purpose-built export split or rebuilding the drafting elements in Vectorworks.

Contents

  1. The three formats, briefly
  2. 1. 3DGS — Vectorworks does not support it
  3. 2. Point cloud — you can measure it, but it has no surfaces
  4. 3. Mesh — it displays, but it is heavy to work in
  5. 4. Build an editable model from a separate hall scan
  6. 5. Connect the editable model to Vectorworks
1. 3DGS→appearance| 2. point cloud→measurement| 3. scan mesh→shape reference| 4. editable model→Blender| 5. drawings→Vectorworks
Test A | Use the city-block scan directlySections 1–3 compare 3DGS, point cloud and scan mesh outputs from the same city-block capture.

The three formats, briefly

A single capture can produce three kinds of data for different jobs.

  • 1. 3DGS — coloured particles recreate a photographic appearance. Best for reviewing and sharing site conditions.
  • 2. Point cloud — measured coordinates represented as dots. Useful for dimensions and tracing.
  • 3. Mesh — triangular surfaces carrying photographs. It has faces, but raw scan meshes are heavy.
Test setupA city block captured with a handheld scanner (XGRIDS Lixel K2), imported into Vectorworks Spotlight 2026. The scan is far too large to handle in one piece, so the mesh was split into three parts and loaded one at a time. The same data was opened in Blender — a widely used 3D application — for comparison.

01 1. 3DGS — Vectorworks does not support it

Vectorworks does not support 3DGS. A 3DGS file stores more than positions — each particle also carries what colour it is, how transparent it is and what shape it takes — but Vectorworks has no way to read any of that. On import it takes only the positions and discards everything else, colour included. What lands on screen is a sparse scatter of near-black dots.

You can bake colour into a conventional point cloud before import, but the view-dependent appearance is lost. The converted result belongs in the next category; it is no longer 3DGS.

02 2. Point cloud — you can measure it, but it has no surfaces

Vectorworks supports point clouds natively, so they import without any conversion. On colour fidelity alone, this is the best of the three.

But 16-bit colour comes out wrongThe file this scanner produced stores colour at a finer precision than usual (16-bit). Open that directly in Vectorworks and building walls come out painted in fluorescent green and bright red — nothing like the real thing. The data itself is not broken; Vectorworks simply cannot read colour at that precision. Convert the colour to the ordinary precision (8-bit) before importing and it displays correctly. The image below is after that conversion.

Points accept snapping, so you can measure distances and place dimensions. But there are no surfaces to select, extrude or cut. Measurement and tracing are where a point cloud stops.

03 3. Mesh — it displays, but it is heavy to work in

A mesh has selectable surfaces and displays its photographic detail. The problem is speed. I opened the same data in Blender for comparison.

TaskVectorworks Spotlight 2026Blender 4.5
LoadingAbout 20–30 secondsTens of seconds
Switching viewAbout 1.5 seconds of waitingNo wait
Other operations0.3–2 secondsFully interactive
Photographic detailDisplays correctlyDisplays without issue

Waiting 1.5 seconds on every view change is genuinely tiresome when drafting means changing the view constantly. But it is not so heavy that it cannot be opened. And this is with only one of the three parts the block was split into — loading the whole scan gets heavier still.

04 4. Build an editable model from a separate hall scan

Test B | Pass an editable model into VectorworksSections 4–5 rebuild a separate hall against its 3DGS and captured images, then import the result as OBJ.

Sections 1–3 above are direct Vectorworks import tests using the city-block scan. I then used a separate hall capture to test a different path: keeping 3DGS and captured images as references while rebuilding editable geometry in Blender. The city block and hall are different datasets; the hall test checks the proposed solution rather than continuing the same import test.

This is not merely a decimated scan mesh. I kept the 3DGS as the comparison baseline and repeatedly matched the same cameras while reconstructing only the required geometry with fewer faces. The model is not yet an exact match, so it remains a rough model that requires manual correction rather than a design or construction model.

The full hall reconstruction workflow and location-by-location comparisons are documented here.

05 5. Connect the editable model to Vectorworks

  • 3DGS — remains the visual and spatial comparison baseline.
  • Captured images — resolve thin parts, wall edges and materials that blur in 3DGS.
  • Editable Blender model — contains only the required geometry, separated by use.
  • Vectorworks — uses the lightweight model as a base for classes, layers, lighting, furniture and drawings.

I exported the hall from Blender 4.5 as OBJ and imported it into Vectorworks Spotlight 2026. The OBJ is 155.6 MB, the MTL is 25.6 KB and the package contains 12 images. The saved Vectorworks file is 109.8 MB.

CheckObserved result
GeometryThe complete hall displayed in both Wireframe and Shaded modes
Object separation1,051 Blender meshes were consolidated into four Vectorworks meshes
TexturesOBJ and MTL alone were insufficient; the 12 images packed in Blender had to be extracted beside the OBJ
Practical useUseful as whole-model shape reference, not as directly editable CAD walls, floors or stage parts
The first import stopped because texture files were missingThe MTL named the images, but the files themselves were packed inside the Blender document. Import completed after extracting all 12 images beside the OBJ. An OBJ delivery therefore needs the OBJ, MTL and referenced images kept together.

Vectorworks 2026 can import OBJ, IFC and point-cloud formats including PLY. PLY support does not mean it preserves Gaussian scale, rotation and opacity. Vectorworks handles it as a point cloud, not as a 3DGS rendering.

IFC is not a better OBJ. It carries BIM meaning such as walls, slabs and storeys. This hall is a mesh without those semantics, so wrapping it in IFC would not automatically turn the geometry into editable building elements. Drafting elements still need to be rebuilt as Vectorworks classes, layers and architectural objects.

The practical result is to review the site in 3DGS, organise only the required geometry in Blender, then pass it into Vectorworks in smaller purpose-based groups. The one-piece OBJ succeeded as shape reference, but it is not a delivery-ready drafting model.
